PROPOSED TAKEOVER OF SUPERTEST BY BRITISH PETROLEUM-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43 I wish to raise a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the government's announcement last night that it has decided not to intervene in the proposed takeover of Supertest by British Petroleum Company Limited. May I be permitted a brief statement before submitting my motion.
Foreign control of the production, refining and distribution of petroleum products has been accelerating at an alarming rate. Canadians are increasingly excluded from the ownership and control of the petroleum and gas industry. The government's inaction can only result in allowing one of our most vital and potentially richest resources falling under foreign domination. Supertest constitutes one of the few remaining Canadian owned outlets for the distribution of petroleum products and steps should be taken to keep it in Canadian hands.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House urges the government to reconsider its decision and take whatever steps are necessary to prevent the takeover of Supertest by the British Petroleum Co. Ltd. in order that the continued acquisition of the petroleum industry by foreign corporations may be brought to a halt.

I have indicated to them that it is impossible to meet their demands and it is absolutely unacceptable for the parents to keep their children out of school. I hope they will reconsider and send their children back to school and then we will be able to negotiate.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday afternoon and last night, we were discussing the question of the $150 exemption which is being permitted to all people for expenses incurred in connection with their work. Members of this party, and some members of the Official Opposition, tired to make the parliamentary secretary understand our concern about what we consider to be the inequities. We tried to point out to the parliamentary secretary that $150 may be too much for some people, but may be much too little for many people.
A number of our members, and also I think the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, pointed out that there are many workers who, because of the housing situation and because of the way in which industries may close factories in one city and open them in another city 25, 50 or 75 miles away, have to travel that distance to and from work. It is not a question of choice for them. Short of disrupting their home life by moving their homes, they have to travel considerable distances to and from work, and this costs them substantially more than $150 a year.
We compared this unfavourably with the treatment given to professional people such as doctors and lawyers. The parliamentary secretary tried to answer our argument on a number of occasions. I do not often quote from Hansard, Mr. Chairman, but here is just one of his statements which summarizes what he tried to tell us. I quote from page 9142 of yesterday's Hansard where the parliamentary secretary was reported as saying:
If hon. members opposite wish to continue to perpetuate the fiction that somehow or other wage and salary earners are discriminated against in that they cannot deduct the cost of travelling to a mill or factory, while professional people are favoured in that they can deduct the cost of going from their homes to their offices, there is nothing I can do to stop them. But it simply is not true.
We never said that we wanted people to be able to deduct their expenses for travelling just for the sake of travelling. We were talking about travel which is necessary if a working man is to do his job. I would like the parliamentary secretary to come to Winnipeg, get up early one morning with me, and drive out to St. Boniface where there are three major packing plants. The first shift starts at seven o'clock in the morning. If a worker is to be at his bench at seven o'clock in the morning, he has got to be in the plant by 6.30 in the morning in order to change clothes and get ready.
This is just one of thousands of examples that I can give. I would like the parliamentary secretary to explain to me how that worker can get to work without using his car. Of course, the parliamentary secretary said somewhat facetiously yesterday that the worker could not charge expenses for the car since it would be sitting out in front of the plant for the rest of the day. Of course, the car sits outside the plant for the rest of the day while the worker is at work. We have tried to make the point again and again that the worker has a problem getting to his job if he does not use his car. His expenses are there.
noon)
I have already put on the record one of the parliamentary secretary's statements to the effect that we are wrong when we say doctors and lawyers can charge car expenses for travelling from home to the office. The parliamentary secretary may be technically correct, but only
Income Tax Act
technically. Doctors are permitted to charge the expenses of their car if they are making calls or going to the hospital. I submit there is no difference between the doctor and the worker who has to drive a considerable distance to work.
I am not an expert in this field so last night I consulted with one of my friends who is an accountant, not with the Department of Finance, but a working accountant who helps doctors, lawyers and others like myself make up their income tax returns. I would like the parliamentary secretary to listen to what my friend told me because I would like an answer. He said that the parliamentary secretary is right, that in recent years the government has become much tougher with regard to doctors and lawyers. Not too many years ago a doctor in any city, Winnipeg, Ottawa or Toronto say, could charge 80 per cent of the expense of his car when calculating his income tax. My friend says that at the present time in Winnipeg, and the same is true of any city in Canada though maybe they are a little easier on rural doctors if there are any left, doctors are permitted to charge 25 per cent of the cost of operating a car.
What does that mean, Mr. Chairman? The cost of operating the car for which they permit the doctor to charge 25 per cent includes gas, oil and automobile insurance. I estimate all this to be in the neighbourhood of $600 or $700 a year. The doctor is also allowed to charge depreciation. My friend the accountant was perhaps a little conservative when he said a doctor may drive a car which costs around $5,000. Most of the doctors I know drive big Buicks and Cadillacs, but let's take that $5,000. In any year the 25 per cent depreciation comes to about $1,250; add the $600 or $700 for gas, oil, maintenance and auto insurance and the doctor is being permitted a deduction of $2,000 a year for his car when calculating his income tax.
I have not got the figures for the average income of doctors in front of me, but as I remember the figures published each year by the Department of National Revenue it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30,000. Many make much more than that, and I estimate that most doctors are in the 40 per cent income tax bracket. By permitting a doctor to charge $2,000 for car expenses he is being given an allowance in the calculation of his income tax not of $150 but more in the neighbourhood of $800. Now, Mr. Chairman, nobody has ever questioned the right of the doctor who wears a white coat or jacket in his office to charge off the cost of buying that, or of laundering it. Yesterday my friend the hon. member for Timis-kaming mentioned the cost of the doctor's scalpel. I am sure doctors use much more sophisticated instruments than scalpels today, Mr. Chairman. That expense is quite legitimate and I am not questioning it. I would not want any member of this House to think that I am questioning the right of the doctor to deduct legitimate expenses when calculating his income tax. What I am saying to the parliamentary secretary, what I said yesterday and what I think the figures I put on the record today demonstrate very clearly, is that in permitting the $150 deduction for everybody for expenses connected with work without the requirement of filing receipts and statements, we do not have any more equity than we have had in the last 25 years or more.

speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary did answer last night, and I regret to say that his answers were very unsatisfactory. It seems to me that he is making some assumptions about the nature of work and the expenses that people incur which do not jibe with the facts of life. Perhaps the people he knows are different from the people I know. I should like to refer to his remarks as recorded at page 9140 of Hansard:
The government makes no attempt to dictate to people where they should live in relation to their place of work.
That is quite true, but as you read the parliamentary secretary's remarks you become aware he assumed that people are quite free to live where they please or to work where they please and therefore if they have to drive to work it is their own fault. It is a very Calvinist kind of attitude to the situation and does not relate to what is happening. Most of the people I know would like to live reasonably close to their place of work. They would also like to have public transportation but the fact is that they cannot have either.
Offices and plants shift, and this government makes no provision for that or for plants shutting down or consolidating. They just say that is the way our society works. But a man cannot shift around that quickly. If he has a house which costs a considerable amount of money it might cost him from $1,000 to $1,800 to sell that house. Perhaps he does not know how long he will be in the next job, so he is caught in the situation where he follows the plant around. It may shift from Galt to Hespeler and from Hespeler to Guelph and often it shifts from one province to another. Today workmen are very specialized which means that they have to secure work in another shop sometimes if their particular shop contracts out part of its operations. The worker does not really have the kind of freedom to choose where he is going to work or where he is going to live that the parliamentary secretary infers. This creates problems because under these circumstances the car becomes an instrument of work just as much as the hard hat or safety shoes.
I am not happy to see this kind of thing take place. I am very much in favour of public transport and I would not want to see any further encouragement of private transport because of all the problems it creates, but nevertheless this anomaly exists in the government. They display one attitude towards the self-employed and professionals and another towards the ordinary workman. I know the government does not take into account the cost of going to and from work, no matter whether professionals or working people are involved. So far, our income tax regulations have not recognized such costs. Those who observe the scene in this country know that it is almost impossible
to say whether a car is being used for professional reasons or for going to work. I realize that the government faces difficulties in this regard, as do those who administer our income tax regulations. Nevertheless, let us admit that fringe benefits so far as automobile use is concerned accrue to some people and do not accrue to others. Let us find a realistic solution to this problem. Let us say, "That is the way the system works for some. In all equity we must give all elements of our population these advantages, regardless of the type of work involved". Let us do that instead of moralizing and saying that it is a workman's fault if he does not live near his job.
Few workmen can choose where they may live in relation to their place of work, particularly in these days of high unemployment. A workman cannot guarantee that he will be working tomorrow; he does not even know where he will be working. He takes a job when it comes up and then looks for ways and means of getting there. It is often difficult for a man to travel to his work. I know of many families that spend 20 per cent of their total budgets on necessary transportation so that the breadwinner can hold down a job. He must spend that much because, without transportation, he cannot hold down the job. Surely, considering all the wisdom that is supposed to reside on the government side of the House which has at its disposal the great brains of the civil service, it ought to be possible to bring in some measure of equity in this regard in order that all persons in our society may be fairly treated under our taxation system.
The grievance I have mentioned will not vanish after passage of this clause. This is a long standing grievance and has been a constant source of irritation to people who must work for a living in the factory or mill, to use the words of the parliamentary secretary. The grievance will continue until some decent arrangement is made with regard to the deduction from taxable income of transportation costs involved in going to work. I am glad to see the parliamentary secretary taking notes. He appears to be listening. The other day he said that he was pleased workmen need no longer live close to the smelly factories in which they must work. What kind of suggestion was he making? Does he think that by moving to the suburbs our people can escape from smog and gasoline fumes? Does he not know that you cannot run away from the effects of air pollution simply by moving away from the factory? His attitude is typical of the sort of Liberal moralizing we have heard in the past. Instead of asking people to move away from the factory, why does the government not remedy the pollution at its source? The effects of pollution are not confined to any geographic area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PART II AND PART III (INCOME TAX APPLICATION RULES, 1971) OF BILL C-259
speechtext: What has the Clean Air Act to do with income tax?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PART II AND PART III (INCOME TAX APPLICATION RULES, 1971) OF BILL C-259
speechtext:
Why not stop factories polluting? After all, there is some relationship between where a person lives and where he works, and I do not think the answer lies in asking people to travel vast distances between where they live and work. In some ways the worker's condition when he lived beside the mill was an unhappy one; yet, in others, it was good. If the mill is polluting the environment, stop the pollution. Do not ask people to
October 29, 1971

move away from the mill. If they move away they will encounter transportation problems. We ought to deal with the problem of pollution at its source. I admit I was most surprised to hear what he said.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary has again failed to grasp the significance of what I am trying to bring to his attention. There is absolutely no difference between an operator or telegrapher relieving at various points throughout his particular seniority (district) and a trainman, bridgeman, sectionman, engineer, conductor and all railway employees who are also relieving for temporary periods of time. I agree that he has a point. If I were trying to create two home terminals, there

would be no argument. But all I am asking is that the same consideration be given in this case as is given to two groups of people already. And all they are doing is relieving. Relieving in the industry as it is today may be for four days, or for a week, or for two weeks. The holiday relief system has assumed increasing importance in recent years. When staff are relieving, they are not exercising seniority. It is not by choice. They are directed by management to go to a particular place to fulfil an obligation the company has undertaken.
I am not asking for the world. All I am suggesting is that we should be consistent-that there should not be two sets of rulings affecting the same people. I wish the hon. member for London East would rise to speak in support of the argument I am putting forward. He knows that this is what happens. We have seen it happen year in and year out, all along the line. I am not asking that special consideration be given to one particular group. I would not try to do that. All I am asking is that consideration be given to people in the railway industry who through no fault of their own are assigned by the company to work away from home. I hope that instead of rejecting this plea out of hand, the parliamentary secretary will agree to take it under further advisement. If he will agree to do so I will certainly be prepared to allow my amendment to stand while he takes a further look at this question.

As a member for the City of Winnipeg, the home of such a large number of railway workers, I rise to join my hon. friend from Moose Jaw in his plea. I was interested to note that this time the parliamentary secretary did not reject the idea which my hon. friend has put forward. He contented himself by observing that it was out of place, that it was advanced at the wrong place in our proceedings.
The railway industry has gone through a revolution since the end of the second world war. The number of employees both in the operating and in the non-operating phase has declined each year. This has often meant major moves for those who have been able to keep their jobs. In his amendment, my hon. friend deals with the case of employees who are required to relieve on a job for a few days or a couple of weeks. I can refer to cases of employees in the dining car department who have lived in Winnipeg for 20 years or more. Because of the reduction in railway service during part of the year, they have been required to work out of Prince Rupert or Vancouver. Nobody has suggested they ought to move their families, because in the summer when business picks up, they are back on the run out of Winnipeg. But for part of the year they must leave their families and move to Vancouver, or anywhere else where employment is awaiting them, not because they wish to move but simply because this is the only way in which they can earn a living.
So the situation arises in which for a certain period, four or five days, two weeks, or even longer, a railway worker whose family is living in one city and incurring expenses for rent and food, must live in another city and bear similar expenses. I could refer to cases where this situation has lasted not for two weeks but for four or five months. There should be equity between different groups of railway workers, equity as between people. No one

questions the right of a salesman to travel across Canada from Winnipeg to Regina, to Calgary, to Vancouver, back to Edmonton and Saskatoon and back to Winnipeg, to charge his expenses for hotel accommodation and meals. I urge the parliamentary secretary and the government to consider favourably what seems to me to be a very reasonable and modest proposal.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think the parliamentary secretary appreciates what it is we are trying to bring to his attention. He asked the hon. member for London East why the railway workers find themselves in this situation. Samuel Freedman discovered that railway workers were in a particular situation, and he had to write a report about it. His report well documented the fact that workers in the railway industry are in a situation that is not found anywhere else.
If I may reply to what the parliamentary secretary said, I am not trying to use one group in a particular industry against another group. I am not trying to have them given favourable recognition under the tax laws which others do not have. Nevertheless, at the present time the expenses of telegraphers and station agents are considered to be a legitimate deduction, as they should be. All I am suggesting is that railway workers should have the same consideration. They are working in every area that serves the needs of their customers. By serving the needs of the customers they are serving the needs of management.
Whether or not this obligation should be placed upon management is something I am sure the collective bargaining process will have to decide at some other time. By the same token, these two classifications are bracketed together in the same collective agreement, and there is no question that they are permanently based at home; they have to move at times in order to serve the needs of management. The situation is the same for this classification of employees as for those we have been speaking about this morning. I contend this group of employees should receive the same treatment. If we were asking for something that was completely unacceptable, or if we were just trying to make a point for the sake of trying to do something for the railway workers, then I could understand the bull-headedness of the parliamentary secretary. But we are not. All we suggest is that there be across the board consideration given to all those railway employees who find themselves in the same situation.
It was suggested a while ago that relieving workers away from home base is something that is particularly akin to telegraphers and station agents but not other classifications of employees, and if that were so I would buy the argument. But it is not so. The number of people who have to move away from home temporarily for a short period is not that high. As suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk, perhaps if the parliamentary secretary could stand this particular item over until after lunch we could make some progress. In fact, if he would stand in his place and indicate what possible difference there is between that group of people who are included and the group of employees to which I and other members have referred, perhaps we could accept his argument. I suggest he is playing with words when he says that one group is relieving from home base and the other group is not relieving from home base. The people now covered are relieving from home base and this is a legitimate deduction. The people we are talking about are also relieving from home base. They all start from the home base, whatever their classification. Those people relieving from home base are in exactly the same situation as those who are covered by the provisions of the act, and they should receive the same consideration in so far as deductions are concerned.
Surely, the parliamentary secretary and his two advisers could come up with a better answer than the suggestion that this amendment is not acceptable to the government because we are not talking about the same thing. We are not talking about employees from airlines but rather employees of railway companies. These employees have to accept an assignment away from home base in order to fulfil an obligation of the company. We are not talking about expenses, and whether expense deductions should be allowed for all employees of the railway companies. I would urge the parliamentary secretary to stand this part of the section and give it serious thought over the noon hour. We are not asking for special concessions for one individual group in the railway industry, but rather the same type of consideration and deductions for all railway employees who are involved in exactly the same type of relief operation.
We are not talking about a transfer to another point or travelling expenses; we are talking about those people who are forced to go 150 miles away from home to man an assignment of the railway company but who receive no consideration for this. They cannot even stay in the bunk-houses any more. They must provide their own accommodation in a private rooming house, a hotel or a motel and pay their own expenses out of their own pockets. This type of deduction is allowed in respect of salesmen and other individuals, and by accepting this amendment we could close a gap that should be closed.
I cannot understand why the parliamentary secretary is trying to confuse this issue by suggesting there are different classifications involved. We are talking about employees in exactly the same circumstances, namely those relieving at a terminal away from home areas where the company requires their services. The provision of these services is in the interest of the entire travelling public and the nation, whether they are provided at the

October 29, 1971

little individual whistle stops or elsewhere. People have to assume these assignments which may involve switching at a brickyard or somewhere else, and we feel the same type of consideration should be given those people involved in relief operations.

It is not a question of procedure with which we are dealing now but rather a question of substance and of justice. For the life of me, I cannot see why the government should be obdurate about something which, from a revenue standpoint, is not apt to be substantial.
From the standpoint of the way in which we deal with the expenses involved in being able to earn a dollar in Canada, this is probably as important and as basic an issue as we can have. The fact is that what is being asked in this amendment, as I understand it, is that if a person should be wrenched away from the family table as it were-and the hon. member for London East I thought put it very well because he had gone through this and the hon. member for Moose Jaw put it very well because he had gone through it also-he should not have to suffer a disability as a result of being forced to go out and get his meals, his living and everything else. Surely, we do not want to just shoot off opinions from the tops of our heads and make judgments on very short notice when perhaps some pretty lengthy deliberation is needed.
The other point I should like to make to my friend the parliamentary secretary, who is a pretty human fellow, is that we are not being asked to overturn the world by accepting a proposition such as this. We are simply being asked to give justice to people who, because of the way in which they earn a living, have to accept a rather different way of life than that of perhaps the parliamentary secretary who would go to his law office in Calgary or I would go to mine if I were practising law at home. These people have to move about. I think these people deserve some extra consideration, and I would hope we would immediately get on to the job of passing sections 4 to 8, while leaving this open for some extra consideration. Mind you, we may come back and still have the government say no, but it is so important an issue that I make this request.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak on this matter since it relates in a small way to the area I represent. The establishment of servo centres for the movement of freight by the railway systems will require a great many employees to travel beyond the communities in which they have established homes, and this is a fundamental, basic reason the government should yield on this point.
It would be no disgrace for the government to admit that members of the opposition once in a while do have some sound ideas, and some pretty basic principles of justice to put forward. I can only add my voice to the many others who have spoken on this. I urge the parliamentary secretary not to force a vote on it, but to yield to reason and allow the amendment to pass.

Mr. Chairman, the views already
expressed in this part of the debate lead me to say a few words. It seems to me that once again we, on behalf of the people of Canada, are giving in to some of the most

powerful organizations in the country, the railways. The hon. member for London East graphically explained the difficulty that he, as an individual, faced. I just cannot understand why the railway companies, on the general principle of fair treatment of their employees, would not take care of this type of problem themselves. Here we are being asked to expand an exception, one which I regard as doubtful in principle. Perhaps instead of expanding section 8(l)(e) we should be restricting it. I fail to see why we should be encouraging through our tax law, a situation in which people are not being given their fair expenses by the companies that employ them. I hope the parliamentary secretary will deal with this matter. I feel that this exception in the statute with respect to telegraphers and station agents is basically wrong in principle, should not be extended further, but should be scrapped. The railway companies, which are probably Canada's most powerful organizations, should not be placed in the position of being able to continue what apparently are very poor labour-management practices.
I also wish to speak on section 8(l)(c) dealing with clergymen's residences. As is well known, there are many large tracts of land in Canada which are held by the churches. One of the reasons they are held in this way is the peculiar tax provisions which we allow to churches and clergymen. If the public which supports churches is willing to pay for a residence, and I think members of that public should, I do not see why we, in turn, after providing a tax deduction for charitable donations to churches, should again give another exception with respect to the residence. I think we should try to put all of this on as fair a basis as possible, so that the tax burden falls more equitably on all members, In that way, members of a congregation can themselves decide, based more on the true cost of a clergyman's residence, to what degree the residence should be supported.
I raise this because of one particular community in Gaspe which I have visited. I know a number of people there. Only 35 per cent of the buildings, residences and property in the town is taxable. All of the other property is either in the hands of the church or of educational institutions. There is a tremendous warping of the tax structure of a municipality when you make all these exceptions for religious and educational purposes. I believe that the people who directly support these establishments should be given a tax rebate for such support. They should not be in a position of getting two sets of tax rebates, as apparently we are providing in section 8(l)(c). It is not my intention to propose an amendment to strike this out, but I think this is a view that should be expressed. It is one that is rarely expressed when we are dealing with taxes that affect church property. Again, I think the parliamentary secretary should comment on why there is this peculiar exception with respect to telegraphers and station agents. I think that in the interests of rationalization it, too, should be struck out.

tunity to read the record of the debate this morning to see if I do understand the point that is being made. I think there has been some element of inequity demonstrated. I think this is an element of inequity as between certain classes of railway employees, that privileges are being granted to telegraphers and relieving station agents, and not to other employees who, in the circumstances and under the conditions mentioned by the hon. member, might merit the same sort of tax treatment. On clause 1-Section 6: Amounts to be included as income from office or employment.

Mr. Chairman, I want once again to raise this matter of the deductions for expenses which workers
Income Tax Act
incur as a result of their employment. For at least 15 or 20 years this has been a matter of great concern to organized workers and has been discussed in the House many times. It is recognized that there is an inequity between wage and salary earners with respect to their right to deduct such expenses from their income tax, and professional groups, travelling salesmen, insurance agents, book agents and others who are able to deduct such expenses.
I must congratulate the government on having finally recognized this problem and trying to do something about it. Our complaint is that the government has followed the usual procedure of bureaucrats in solving the problem by saying that the $150 exemption will be granted to every employee irrespective of what their expenses are in connection with their employment. This $150 exemption will apply where the only thing a man has to buy in order to do his work is a ball point pen as compared to a logger who has to buy a power saw which could cost anywhere from $300 to $600. It will apply equally to a man who lives a few blocks from a plant and can get there by bus and to a man who has to drive 30 or 40 miles. It seems to me that the government could have done a much better job in resolving this problem This is the Procrustean bed theory. You force everybody into the same bed; if they are too short, you stretch them and if they are too long, you lop a piece off without any regard to the circumstances, equity or justice.
I want to draw the minister's attention to two groups in my constituency who will be adversely affected by the inequities of this provision. The first is the men who work in the logging camps. They have to buy special equipment, hard hats, special work boots and they have to provide their own power saws in most cases. This involves an expenditure far in excess of $150 a year. In addition, many have to drive very long distances to work. I know that in subsection 7 there is a definition of a special work site. Under certain conditions a man may claim travelling expenses as an exemption. The special site is confined either to something of a temporary nature, which I take it means simply a construction site and would not cover a logging camp which could operate for several years, or some place where the taxpayer could not reasonably be expected to establish and maintain a domestic establishment. This is going to raise a good deal of controversy.
In my constituency there are logging camps where accommodation is provided for single men. There is limited accommodation for families so men drive 20, 30 or 40 miles morning and night to these camps. They really have no choice in the matter, as it is doubtful that they could get accommodation at the camps. In many cases they already own a home. It is surely not suggested that they try to dispose of their home and move into a bunkhouse in a logging camp. It seems to me that some provision should be made for such a group.
The second group of employees for whom this provision constitutes an injustice is the longshoremen. They have no choice of where their operation may be. A man may live in Chemainus and then he has just the ordinary travelling expenses of going to the docks. But at any time he can be ordered to a port 50, 70 or 80 miles away; he must travel there, work all day, and return at night. Certainly, a port 50 miles away will not constitute a special work site because it is not temporary. He could get housing accom-

October 29, 1971
Income Tax Act
modation there but he may only work there for two or three days.
Considering all the thought the government has given to this tax reform legislation, I would have expected the tax experts to come up with something much better than this uniform exemption of $150. In some cases it is unnecessary and in the cases I have cited, as well as many others, it is grossly inadequate and certainly unfair. I can only conclude that either the personnel of the Department of Finance and the minister and his parliamentary secretary have not consulted at all with the people who are familiar with the working conditions of Canadians or they would surely have proposed a better provision than the one presently before us.
I should like to appeal to the minister to revise the definition of the circumstances under which a worker would be entitled to travelling expenses and to board and lodging. The limitation is too narrow. A great many workers have to travel long distances and be absent from home, but they will not qualify under this legislation and will not be allowed to deduct the expenses incurred as a proper exemption under the Income Tax Act. .
I hope that before section 6 is allowed to pass the government will undertake to make some changes in order to increase the number of persons to whom exemption will be granted with respect to board and lodging and travelling expenses necessarily incurred in order to carry out the duties related to their employment.

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks of the previous speaker, I should like to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) that all told this $150 maximum amount of expenses allowed for tax deduction will represent for the ordinary worker a tax reduction of only $20 or $25, which I believe totally inadequate.
Besides, we have begged for many years in the House for such a taxation relief, and the government always turned a deaf ear when it came to workers. In fact, I stated myself in this House that there was shameless discrimination against the worker. One must consider that other professional groups, such as insurance agents, businessmen, doctors and dentists have the right to deduct from their gross income the cost of their equipment and all travelling expenses incurred in the discharge of their duties.
Workers are right to protest against injustice because I believe that the lumbermen, both in my constituency and throughout Canada, are entitled to a better treatment. Everyone knows that today the lumberman's work is so mechanized that he must spend thousands of dollars to buy machines such as mechanical saws, etc., but he will be allowed to deduct only $150 from his total income. I ask the parliamentary secretary to give more consideration to this group of workers who make up almost 85 per cent of the labour force in the area. In fact, only 15 per cent of the workers will get anything out of this while an injustice will be committed against the others who quite often are the most in need because they earn less.

For example, I am thinking of the plumber or mechanics whose tools may cost up to $1,000 or $1,500. These tools must be constantly renewed so that the amount of $1,000 which could be deducted for tax purposes would be over a period of two or three years. This gives you an idea of the cost of those workers' tools, which I call third-class workers, in relation to those who have been granted advantages by the government and who managed to have special laws passed to enjoy tax exemptions. I wonder whether this was not due to their influence in this Parliament against the workers of our regions.
I believe they exerted a great influence and had great supporters. I have no grudge against them! I have nothing against the professional classes because I myself as a merchant am very happy to be able to deduct travelling expenses incurred while looking after my business.
However, I want as much fairness for everybody and I want those workers to be in a position to deduct the cost of their tools and their transportation. It must be realized that the worker no longer lives in a lumber camp today, that he uses his car in the morning to cover 70, 75 or even 80 miles in order to cut wood the whole day long and returns at night, because lumber camps are no longer maintained, as in the past, when the lumberman "hibernated" for four, five or six months, in short, as long as the contract lasted.
Today, because work stops on Friday afternoon, the worker must come back to town, return home on the weekend because there is no cook at the camp.
He cannot even be repaid, if only one third of the expenses related to his work.
I could talk about all the other trades which do not seem to be considered in this bill. It seems to me that this would have given the minister a unique opportunity to say: At last, justice will be done to them. For the last seven or eight years, the government has been urged to try and give justice to this group of workers who will be voting in a proportion of 85 per cent in the next election.
This group is large enough, Mr. Chairman, for the minister and his parliamentary secretary to give them consideration, and I urge the government, before passage of those sections, to give them a second thought and not to think only of themselves but also of those who elected them. They deserve some sort of tax relief once in a while.
I do not want to take up too much time, but I could not let this section be passed without calling upon the minister and asking him to amend it so that all will be treated equally. All I am asking for is an act of social justice. In fact, we heard it so often said during the last election campaign: Fellow Canadians, from now on, we will have a just society.
We are calling for a positive act of social justice for the workers. We are not asking for special exemptions but only what has been always granted to the others. They have a right to an equal treatment and let us stop making this group that makes up 95 per cent of the population a group of underprivileged citizens, a third class group in our society.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will note those remarks and that before passage of this section, he will introduce something more sensible, more positive and more equitable.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two about subparagraph (e) of subsection 6(1) and about subsection 6(2), entitled respectively, "standby charge for automobile" and "reasonable standby charge minimum amount". I want to relate my remarks to people employed particularly as salesmen for automobile firms. I will not go into the question of whether there should be such a charge or not. It has been brought to my attention that some salesmen employed by automobile firms are required, as part of their duties, to drive cars as demonstrators. The value of these cars may vary greatly. One day a car salesman may demonstrate a car selling for $2,000 and the next day he may demonstrate one selling for $7,000 or $8,000. In the case of salesmen of this type it would be impossible to apply these provisions in any equitable way.
Also, salesmen like these are in a different position from, say, salesmen selling products for Burns & Company, a furniture company, or some company like that. In other words, the vehicle supplied to such salesmen for their own use is the vehicle which they are selling. It is the merchandise which they are selling and they are, therefore, in a position different from that of a salesmen to whom automobiles are supplied. As a result, there ought to be included in the bill a provision exempting them from the particular subsections I have referred to; or some type of special provision ought to be introduced to make sure they will not be unfairly discriminated against and placed in an impossible situation in determining what they ought to pay. I hope the government will make a modification along the line I have suggested. I should like to hear what the parliamentary secretary has to say about this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the particular matter raised by the hon. member for Calgary Centre was brought to the government's attention yesterday by a delegation, perhaps the same group which saw the hon. member. Certainly, it is recognized there is a genuine problem here. We are looking at it. At this time, I cannot indicate what the solution might be. However, I can assure the hon. member that it is being given very serious consideration. As I say, unfortunately it was only flagged for us very recently.
Mr. Chairman, might I ask if we can take it for granted that this section will not be finally passed until some amendment is introduced in connection with the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that is an agreeable solution to the problem. We intend to face up to it. It is going to require some study in order to determine the magnitude of the problem. As the hon. member may know, the suggestion has come forward from the people who are concerned with this problem that a flat amount of some sort or other be assessed each month or each year in order to take care of the situation where the gentleman is driving a Cadillac one day and a Volkswagen the next, because the computation problems would obviously be somewhat horrendous. I can only say at this point I am not prepared to suggest we will necessarily have the solution by the time we feel that the bill should be passed. I do
Income Tax Act
not think this solves the problem, but we will look for a solution.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak briefly on this. This is a classic example of the way the government trys to deal with something. They think they have a problem and, in dealing with it, they create more problems. There is one other area on which I would like to speak very briefly. I will refer back to section 74(3) and (4) and also section 63; this deals with the worker's employment allowance. A married woman working for a firm which is owned by her spouse, one that is not incorporated or in which her spouse is a partner, provides the services of an employee but will be denied the worker's allowance because she is not considered to be an employee. As I said, by trying to do something, the government is creating more problems.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to return for a few minutes to the subject matter recently raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and followed up by the hon. member for Roberval. If the congenial parliamentary secretary is becoming a little weary over the persistence with which this matter is being discussed, I remind him that this Pandora's box, if that is what he regards it as being, was opened by the government in the white paper.
The provision in the white paper of this flat rate $150 deduction for those in receipt of employment income was put forward and at that time was hailed by the Minister of Finance as being a great reform in the tax system. If I recall correctly, when we had the discussion on the white paper, I was the first member in the House to jump on that proposal with both feet. I remember the rather startled look on the faces of some of the government members when I condemned it out of hand. I concede that as I read the white paper, it appeared to me that this $150 proposal was being put forward as a substitute for the partial recognition of board, lodging and travelling expenses which exist in the present Section 5 of the Income Tax Act which had reference only to construction workers. Some hon. members will recall that particular proposal was brought forward and put into the act in 1957 by the first Conservative Minister of Finance when the right hon. member for Prince Albert was Prime Minister. It has remained in that position ever since.
As one read the white paper, it appeared that that concept, partially recognized in the present Section 5 of the act, was to be removed and this $150 flat rate was to be put in its place. As I said in the committee discussion yesterday, I am happy that that surmise on my part has not proven to be correct when the bill came forward, whether or not, as a result of the representations made concerning it at the time. However, recognition was given to what I consider to be the grossest discrimination against people whose income comes from employment. I remind the parliamentary secretary through you, Mr. Chairman, that it was on the initiative of the government that this proposal was put forward. The more one talks about it, the more unrealistic and unfair that proposal is in its present form. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands pointed out, some workers will really get a bonanza as a result of this proposal. When we were discussing the white paper, I said it brought in a new

October 29, 1971
Income Tax Act
form of discrimination against some of the people who are self-employed. To that extent at least, one can regard it as a retrogressive step.
Last night I listened to some members of my party and members in other parts of the House who come from urban areas discussing this particular proposal. They tried to point out this weakness. The parliamentary secretary attempted to provide a rationale for the proposal as it stands. I admit he made a valiant attempt, but he certainly did not convince me he was on the right track in his thinking in the arguments he presented.
I wish to come back to the point made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at the very outset of this current phase of discussion on the bill. He quite properly drew a parallel between the $150 proposal as a basic exemption and the existing plan with regard to medical expenses. All taxpayers are able to claim a $100 fait rate if that, in fact, covers the incidental medical expenses they have incurred. However, if they have the documentation necessary under the regulations, they can claim an additional amount if, in fact, they have incurred additional expenses over and above the minimum amount. It seems to me that when it brought forward this $150 proposal in the white paper the government failed to recognize the principle which has been generally accepted as being reasonable, fair and just with respect to medical expenses. For the life of me, I cannot see why the government is not prepared to recognize the same principle in the case of transportation expenses.
When arguments have been presented in the past in favour of improvements in the law, they have often been resisted on the grounds that administration would be difficult or costly. This used to be the reply to proposals which some of us put forward in the House for the establishment of a pension plan. The position today is that a great many calculations, including calculations in respect of income tax returns, are put through computers and this has opened up a whole new range of administrative possibilities when dealing with large numbers of forms. In the light of this development, I believe that properly vouchered claims for transportation expenses should not be too difficult for the administration to handle. Having gone so far as to make this $150 flat rate proposal, the government should now be prepared to go the rest of the way to make it possible for workers who have a bona fide claim to expenses above that level to receive proper consideration.
The parliamentary secretary can advance all the arguments he likes about it not being the responsibility of the government to decide where a person should live in relation to his job. But the fact of the matter remains that in both urban and rural areas workers who may be able to stay in their own homes every night must, of necessity, incur substantial travelling expenses. This is the only way in which our industrial machine can continue to operate. I am sure it is possible for those who devise the working rules under which the Income Tax Act is administered to work out the necessary regulations and requirements with regard to documentation so that a proposal which would meet the situation outlined by my hon. friend from Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands could be put forward.

In my view, it would be more equitable for the government to withdraw this $150 flat rate proposal altogether than to leave the clause as it is, because it is simply not fair that all workers should be put into this same box; it is simply not fair that this formula of the 3 per cent or $150 maximum should be attached. As the arrangement stands, it means that the lower income workers will suffer the heaviest discrimination. I have in mind workers who must travel long distances in order to secure or to hang on to a job. It will be the least well established members of the work force who are likely to be the most heavily penalized under this proposal. I do not know whether my hon. friends agree with me or not, but I would personally prefer to see the whole thing forgotten rather than write this $150 thing into the bill as it now stands.

It is obvious that the minister and the parliamentary secretary will, in any case, have an opportunity to consider this question overnight, at least. I should like to know what we are talking about. How much money are we talking about? Is it a sizeable sum? The sum of $150 has been used as a cut-off. What does the 3 per cent amount to? Are predictions as to the probable cost available? What escalation has there been during the last ten years in this field? Are we getting into it deeper, or getting into it less than was the case previously and, if so, what is the cost of this proposition to the treasury? I am sure this just did not come out of a hat, this figure of $150 or the 3 per cent figure. On second thought I am not so sure but, hopefully, the department does have some figures as to what this proposal would cost.
We have drawn an analogy between professionals and the labour force with regard to the tools of their trade. And we have pointed out that not all the returns made are beyond question. The minister is always sending inspectors around the country to assess the validity of some of the claims made by those in the self-employed and professional fields. So I ask the parliamentary secretary to tell us, if he can, whether or not the proposal advanced from this corner of the House can be adopted without great cost to the treasury.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext: that Bill S-9 to amend the Copyright Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill merits some brief explanation here, although I recognize there is a general disposition in the House to deal with it expedi-
October 29, 1971

tiously because of some deadlines of which all hon. members are aware.
The purpose of this bill is to remove any legal right that may exist for record manufacturers to obtain royalties through the use of a performing right on their records. As hon. members may know, composers, authors and publishers of music have a right to charge for the public performance of their works. This is an inherent part of the Copyright Act and results in substantial annual payments being made to these groups of persons. Each year the performing rights societies file a proposed tariff of fees with the Copyright Appeal Board which in turn assesses and fixes the fees that are to be paid to them by users for the public performance of their works. This right allows these societies to examine the financial records of the users and to extract a fee based on the gross revenue, in many cases, of the user.
Four years ago an additional performing rights society was created, that of Sound Recording Licenses Ltd. This society consisted of a group of some 18 Canadian record companies, approximately 90 per cent of the record manufacturers in Canada but which are principally subsidiaries of foreign corporations. In due course they claimed a "performing right" in their sound recordings, a right that is distinct and apart from any right they had to prevent the copying of their records by others. The result would be to exact from the Canadian broadcasting industry rather substantial fees for their use of recorded music.
Their claim to a performing right is based on a technical and complex provision of the present Copyright Act which the bill now before the House amends. While the original tariff of fees filed with the Copyright Appeal Board would have resulted in fees payable somewhere in excess of $3 million per year, the Copyright Appeal Board allowed a somewhat lower fee. However, the question is really one of the principle that no performing right should exist in a record, that is, the purely mechanical apparatus upon which sound or images are recorded, as distinct from the intellectual and human input to those products. They are already taken care of by the other performing rights societies.
In 1966 the government asked the Economic Council to study the law of copyright and its economic effect upon Canadians. Subsequently they were specifically asked to consider the question of performing rights for record manufacturers. The Economic Council reported its findings this spring and it reaffirmed the recommendations of the Ilsley Commission in its report on copyright in 1957 which recommended that the act be amended to ensure that no such performing right could be claimed. While the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford) would have preferred to await a complete overhaul of the Copyright Act before considering this matter, the fact is that the Copyright Appeal Board awarded a tariff to SRL this spring and it is the government's feeling that such a tariff is in principle wrong.
It should be pointed out that there is no conflict with any international obligations we may have under copyright, nor does the United States, where the parent companies of SRL's member firms are located, have such a provision in its copyright legislation, although there is at
Copyright Act
present and has been for some years a bill before the United States Congress which would change that. I am led to believe that it has little likelihood of passage.
SRL has offered to keep a substantial part of the money in Canada and has also offered to pay a part of any fees collected to the musicians who record the music. While this is admirable, it is an attempt to evade the issue. If the singers and musicians who make a recording should have a performing right, that is something that should be dealt with on its own and not through the back door of providing a performing right and a tariff for the record companies.
It should be made clear that the government is not denying copyright protection to records. The protection of records against copying exists in our law and will continue to exist. Bill S-9 does not affect the protection provided record companies against copying or against piracy. However, in the government's view that is all the record companies are entitled to. It is the government's position that even though the Copyright Appeal Board allows only a small fee now, SRL recently filed a new tariff of fees and applied for a substantial increase in its tariff. It is wrong, therefore, to allow a totally new vested interest to be built up at this time and it is now that appropriate steps must be taken. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, the government asks the co-operation of the House in disposing of this very important item of legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government, as is usual, of course, will have the co-operation that it seeks in processing this legislation. However, it is something of an anomaly that in the case of the grain stabilization act the excuse given for not proceeding with the bill was that there was a court action, while in the case of this bill a court action is to be nullified by statute. I suppose it depends which band you play in.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext:
I am not going to waste part of Friday afternoon on an argument of semantics; I should just like the anomaly brought to the attention of the House. We are going to co-operate because we feel that this is really a matter for debate by, or a battle to be fought between two very large and important interests, interests that the government has to adjudicate upon or with regard to which it must act as referee.
I agree with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) that it is a very great pity that the fundamental reform of the Copyright Act has not yet seen the light of day in spite of the fact that since the Copyright Act of 1921 there have been numerous royal commissions and studies, the latest of which was a most excellent report published by the Economic Council of Canada. This was a report on intellectual and industrial property which at page 258 gives a very lucid exposition of the principle that this bill is designed to embody.
As the parliamentary secretary said, we are not dealing here with the fundamental rights of singers and musicians; hopefully, their rights will be underlined in legislation that will have to come before the House at a later date. However, when the bill gets to committee, presumably the rights of singers, musicians and performers as

October 29, 1971
Copyright Act
enunciated by ACTRA and other trades union organizations will be aired, and doubtless SRL and other such organizations will also want to appear before the committee.
Copyright consists of an exclusive right in a musical, literary or dramatic work. A necessary consequence is that such work may not be reproduced except by permission of the copyright owner. Secondly, copyright consists of a performing right in the work so that no one may perform the work except upon payment of a royalty to the copyright owner.
In 1921, upon a revision of the Canadian Copyright Act, parliament enacted in subsection (3) of section 4-the provision we are dealing with here-that copyright should subsist in records, perforated rolls and other contrivances by means of which sounds may be mechanically reproduced in like manner as if such contrivances were musical, literary or dramatic works. This provision was copied from the United Kingdom prototype and, as the parliamentary secretary has reminded us, there is no such provision in the copyright law of the United States.
It is my understanding-I think the parliamentary secretary mentioned this in his brief remarks-that there has been for some time a bill on this issue before the United States Congress. I presume that if this Parliament did deal with the issue it would mean that increasing pressure would be brought to bear to move along the bill in the United States Congress. No one appeared to assert performing rights under the provision, which is perhaps not strange because it really has something to do with the whole expansion of the recording industry. There was no assertion of the right from 1921 until 1968. In that year, Sound Recording Licenses-a consortium of the eight major record companies in Canada of which six are subsidiaries of United States companies-a Canadian company, filed an application with the Copyright Appeal Board for approval of a tariff. The parliamentary secretary has told us of the outcome.
[DOT] <3:10 p.m.)
In 1968 the government introduced Bill S-20. I am sorry to take a minute or two on this matter but I think that the bill having come to us from the Senate, when future historians are trying to discover what we were doing on October 29, 1971, they will need some historical perspective in this regard. I will take a minute or two to bring the House up to date on the various emphases, and so on, placed on this question. I can assure the Parliamentary Secretary that there will be no difficulty, in so far as this party is concerned, in giving the bill second reading in the time allocated.
The government introduced in the Senate Bill S-20, the prototype of Bill S-9 which we are discussing. There was an explanation given in the records of the other place. I am not going to use that cliche any longer. I prefer to call the Senate, the Senate because that is a perfectly sensible word. I will hereinafter refer to the Senate as the Senate and to Senators as Senators. I believe that the ancient system of discussing that part of Parliament as "the other place" is unnecessary.
There was a short debate on second reading during which the opposition House leader questioned the principle of the action the government was taking, and on

February 6, 1969, the government withdrew the bill. This action was taken in agreement with SRL, which undertook not to proceed with its tariff application until the Economic Council of Canada reported on the reference made to it to study the question. The government was anxious to have the advice of the Economic Council. That advice covered many aspects but in particular the government was seeking advice about the whole copyright field.
It might be of interest to recall that in June, 1954, a royal commission under distinguished Chief Justice Ilsley, a great Nova Scotia parliamentarian, had been appointed to inquire into patents, copyright, trademarks and industrial designs. This report was printed in 1957, but unfortunately very little action followed. In other words, there was the usual non-action on the part of successive governments to the activities of royal commissions. The commission recommended that copyright subsisting in a sound recording should continue to subsist but for a period of 40 rather than 50 years from the first publication, but that record manufacturers' performing rights and broadcasting rights in records or in the recording embodied in the record should be abolished.
The Economic Council reference was ordered in July, 1966, and it reported five years later. The Economic Council recommended that the performing right in a sound recording should be removed. However, the chairman of the council, in a preface to the report, advised that two members of the council could not concur completely with the analysis and recommendations on copyright. Then, as the parliamentary secretary has said, SRL revised its application to the Copyright Appeal Board applicable to the year beginning January, 1971. Then in December of 1970 the government introduced Bill S-9. It will be rioted that clause 2 provides that the bill is to take effect January 1, 1971. So the principle embodied in the bill has had a rather chequered career; it came forward and was dropped almost as fast as Parliaments come and go.
The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce. At the second meeting of the committee the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) appeared for the purpose of announcing that the Copyright Appeal Board had granted the SRL claim and fixed a scale of tariffs. That is really the chronology, although other members may be interested in different aspects of this matter which they will want to discuss. I want to underline on behalf of this party the comment of the parliamentary secretary, that in no way does the Official Opposition wish to see the right of a singer or musician circumscribed or nullified in any way by this bill, and that issue must be faced in spite of what Parliament may do with this legislation.
There is a second aspect which I am sure will grip the attention of hon. members even more than those first few minutes of chronological presentation. I refer to the constitutional aspect of the bill. Under the British North America Act, copyright comes under paragraph 23 of section 91-that great division of powers-but there it simply states that it is, in legal effect, a subtraction from the exclusive provincial authority to legislate upon property and civil rights in the province. We are advised in this regard, although the courts are not allowed to look to the draftsmen for help in interpreting the constitution-and
October 29, 1971

this is an anomaly that some day Parliament might get around to reforming.
The draftsmen of the BNA Act had before them for guidance two existing constitutions, that of the United Kingdom and, equally important to the draftsmen, the federal system as it was in effect in the United States. The United Kingdom, because of its unitary nature, has authority over property and civil rights. Within this broad scope the United Kingdom Parliament can define "copyright" in its own terms, either limited to the accepted conceptual idea of copyright or artificially and, therefore, conceptually inexact.
The attention of the draftsmen of the BNA Act was no doubt also directed to article 1, section 8 paragraph 8 of the Constitution of the United States. That paragraph empowers Congress to promote the progress of science and the useful arts by securing for limited times to authors and inventors the exclusive rights to their restrictive writings and discoveries. Whatever the inspiration, however, in respect of the copyright part of the British North America Act, I think it is important to take a minute or two to remember this bit of historical background when considering the bill before us.
Parliament, in the definition in the bill that we are considering today, appears to be saying that sound recordings are not original musical, literary, dramatic or artistic works as defined in section 2 of the Copyright Act. The point of taking an extra minute or two was only to once again emphasize how essential it is for us to consider at an early date the whole matter of the right of a singer, a musician or other artist. The philosophy, if I can put it that way, of this bill has had fairly thorough examination by the Senate. It also has the merit of being reinforced by the report on intellectual and industrial property.
There is one other aspect which I should like to discuss in a sentence or two to remind the House that the SRL's dividing the spoils, if I can put it this way, really does not mean that those spoils accrue to the benefit of Canada. As a matter of fact, the division will largely be made by the American Union of Musicians. I am not entering into a philosophical debate on international unionism but am reminding the House that the division of those funds will take place under a formula worked out by the American Union of Musicians and the various other trade unions and groups representing not only musicians but the technical people who are involved in the making of recordings.
Therefore, when we think about the bill I believe we should ask ourselves where the benefit will accrue, or what I might call the windfall. In other words, there would be a windfall if this legislation is not passed. A substantial part of this windfall would accrue to the United States of America. Here, as a caveat, I say I am not conducting a rather unpleasant discussion such as has been going on in this country vis-a-vis the United States; I am just saying that a very large amount of money which until 1968 had never been the subject of an assertion would accrue and be distributed to the benefit largely of another country.
I urge the government with its experience and, as the parliamentary secretary said, having to meet a deadline,
Copyright Act
to let the whole subject matter of copyright law be subject to a good and progressive piece of reform legislation. With that admonition and with the suggestion that we are really dealing with an adjudication between two variable interests, I may say that we support the bill. We hope that these large interests will have an opportunity for their day in court, so to speak, before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and that the fundamental right of those whom we should seek to help-that is, the performers-will be kept very much in mind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the explanation of the government's position by the parliamentary secretary and the rather interesting subcommentary by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) I am inclined to support the motion that the bill receive second reading and go to committee. I was worried for a while when the negotiations were under way that perhaps the bill would not go to a standing committee for examination and that it was the intention of the government to seek to have all stages concluded in the House. I would think, despite the impression I have that justice lies essentially with the performers and that on balance we should be supporting their position rather than that of the recording companies, the recording companies have a right to appeal to the Commons directly and to have their case heard.
There is an interesting aspect to this bill. The Commons really is being asked to adjudicate between two conflicting pecuniary claims. The government has taken the position that the income of performers should be protected and should not be diminished by the inclusion of the recording companies in this field. I have stated our feelings on the matter and we are quite prepared to see the bill go to committee and receive quick passage thereafter.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RECORDS, PERFORATED ROLLS OR OTHER CONTRIVANCES FOR MECHANICALLY REPRODUCING SOUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this bill. I take this opportunity to remind the government, as I have on many occasions in the past, that it is high time we got down to serious business and revised not only the Copyright Act, which is about 60 years old, but also the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act and the Industrial Design and Union Label Act.
We talk a great deal about the economy, labour and finance of this country, but the Acts to which I refer are all restrictive to our economy. They make it possible for Canadians to export as royalties or otherwise about 60 per cent, 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the income derived under them to foreign countries, and to restrict the use by Canadians of patents of inventions, processes of manufacturing, and so on; trademarks in the use of words and copyrights to perform or to use reading matter in the case of books. I would have hoped, especially after all the royal commissions that were in action 10, 12 or 15 years ago, and after the reports of these commissions and of the Economic Council of Canada, that at this time we would seriously be discussing not a simple amendment, important as it may be, but new legislation which would be drafted in the interest of Canadian citizens.
A great deal has been made about everyone wanting to be a great Canadian nationalist; but we are still servants, under so many of these acts, to our foreign competitors and producers. I hope the government will look at this

October 29, 1971
Copyright Act
particular type of legislation as well as the other legislation which affects our lives but perhaps not as directly from an economic point of view as the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act, the Industrial Design and Union Label Act and the Copyright Act. In the meantime I would remind the government that it is well for it to participate in some of the international meetings relating to the protection of industrial property but not to be in too much of a hurry to sign agreements which would make it impossible at a future time to draft laws relating to copyright which should be in the interest of Canadians. I have already attended a number of such conferences. Our hands are already tied in respect of many international agreements. Let us not be in too much of a hurry in the future to agree until we have drafted an act which is in the interest of all Canadians.
This legislation apparently is necessary because action by the SRL would impose another burden on broadcasters in Canada, and surely any burden on them means more expense on the part of our citizens who will have to contribute to the expenses of the broadcasters. For these reasons I hope this bill will be given second reading immediately and be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
