speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: DESIGNATION OF SPEAKER AS MEMBER FOR PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
that Bill C-52, respecting the designation of the Speaker of the House of Common as the member for the electoral district of Parliament Hill, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting afternoon. I shall certainly underline the things that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) said about me when I get a copy of today's Hansard. I also want to express my thanks to the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) for once again seconding my motion with respect to this bill.
Another preliminary remark I should like to make is that I hope I can be permitted, for the sake of the record, to draw attention to the fact that when during the course of this debate we address you, Sir, as Mr. Speaker, it is Your Honour, Mr. Deputy Speaker, who is in the chair at this time. In other words, I am drawing attention to the fact that we are debating this matter in the absence of His Honour the Speaker himself, and I think that is as it should be.
The purpose of this bill, as hon. members are fully aware, is to open the question of finding a way to provide for a continuing Speakership. This is a matter that has been discussed a good many times over the years. It gets the most serious discussion when we have in the chair an occupant such as the present Speaker. I am sure that all of us in this House feel that this institution itself is the better for the kind of leadership being given to us by today's occupant of the chair-and because of that leadership, because of what His Honour does for us, I suggest that right now there is even more discussion than usual on the desirability of finding a way to provide for a continuing Speakership.
I confess I have to express some regret that with the next election probably not more than a year away, no formal steps seem to have been taken to make sure that the present incumbent will be in the chair when we come back after the next election. I still hope that some way may be found to make this possible, and in particular I would hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the leader of this House, would meet for discussions with the leaders of the other parties to see if something cannot be done to achieve this desirable end.
Sir, with respect to the bill itself I should like to say that I have given the matter a good deal of thought and I have discussed it with a good many people. I have no hesitation in saying that I think the provisions that are spelled out in my bill meet the various problems and that my bill represents the best solution of this matter that has yet been put forward. At the same time, I want to say that my concern is not with the details that I have put into this bill but with the principle. It will not offend me at all if persons speaking on this bill find details in it that they think should and could be improved. Indeed, I would welcome any other
October 29, 1971

device that might be brought forward as a means of achieving the purpose. However, I hope that if anyone is going to propose another device or another bill it will be something that is better than this one, something that copes with the problems that in my bill I have endeavoured to resolve.
Having said that may I, just for the purposes of the Hansard record, indicate the way my bill would provide for a continuing Speakership. The bill is entitled, "An act respecting the designation of the Speaker of the House of Commons as the member for the electoral district of Parliament Hill." It would provide that when a Member of Parliament has been elected in the normal way and has subsequently been elected to the chair by the House of Commons-the way we have done it for over 100 years as spelled out in the British North America Act-that that incumbent once he had two full sessions in the chair could, by a resolution of the House of Commons, be designated as the member for Parliament Hill.
May I make the point that that is an optional provision; the House would not have to do it. It would be free to do it if it was satisfied, as we are in this Parliament, with the job being done by the person in the chair. But in any case, the resolution to declare an incumbent of the chair the hon. member for the electoral district of Parliament Hill could be made only in the case of a member who had been in the chair for two full sessions. The present occupant has many more sessions than that. If this bill were to become law, of course it could be applied immediately in this case.
The step that would immediately follow from the designation of Mr. Speaker as the member for the electoral district of Parliament Hill would be that the constituency that had elected him at the previous election would be declared vacant and a by-election would be called there in the normal way. This is achieved in my bill by having, in addition to the amendments it makes to the British North America Act, the amendment that it makes to the Canada Elections Act. Thus, a vacancy having been declared in the constituency from which His Honour the Speaker had come, that constituency could hold a by-election and elect another member who would be a voice for that constituency on the floor of the House of Commons.
My bill expressly provides that in that circumstance Mr. Speaker, as the member for the electoral district of Parliament Hill, is a full member of the House of Commons in every other way. Indeed, it provides that the number of members of the House of Commons would be one more than is normally the case. In other words, if this bill were made law and came into effect at the present time, a new member would be elected for Stormont-Dundas and there would be a total of 265 seats in the House of Commons.
This bill goes on to provide that at the time of dissolution Mr. Speaker, who even under the present law continues in his office as the person in charge of staff and other arrangements in the House of Commons, would continue to be the member for the electoral district of Parliament Hill. He would not have to run anywhere to continue to hold that membership. He would be that member until the day the next Parliament, following an intervening election, meets as required by law to elect its Speaker. At that
Designation of Speaker
point my bill provides that he would be an eligible candidate for the Speakership of that new Parliament.
I trust it is clear from the way I put it that it would not be automatic; he would not be forced upon the succeeding Parliament. Presumably he would know and everyone else would know from what had happened in the previous Parliament whether it was likely he would be wanted. That being the case, the incumbent of the chair could carry on. He would be free, if he did not want to exercise that right, to run in a normal constituency and revert to the more normal role of us ordinary mortals who make up this chamber.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, while there are arguments about whether Mr. Speaker throughout his time in the chair should be a member in the sense that the rest of us are, having connections with a constituency, the argument comes down on the side of the proposition that the Speaker should in the first place be an ordinary Member of Parliament, should know what it is to run and get elected, perhaps run and get defeated and all the rest. But I think there comes a time when the incumbent of the chair has done such a good job, as is the case with the present incumbent, that it means more to Parliament as a whole to have him continue in that role than to put him in the position of having to go back and run in a partisan contest at a succeeding election.
I said earlier, and perhaps I may be permitted to repeat it, that the time when one considers this sort of thing, the time when it is most desirable to consider it, is when one has a person in the chair concerning whom there is a unanimous feeling of support and respect. You do not get a continuing Speaker-and you note that I prefer that word to the word "permanent", a bit of semantics I suppose but I cannot see anyone being a permanent fixture although I can see a continuing operation-by just deciding to one day go out and pick up a university professor or a worn-out politician, or a brand new one either, and put him in the chair. He might succeed or fail, no matter what his recommendations may have been.
You get a satisfactory continuing Speakership by seizing the moment when you have someone in the chair who is doing the job, who has proven his capacity, and saying that now is the time to continue this relationship. That is why I think there is a fair amount of discussion about the matter at the present time and I hope the discussion this afternoon will indicate that there is support for finding a way of putting this idea into practice before the next election.
As I have already said, I think my bill meets the various problems and meets them well. However, I do not have the kind of pride of authorship that would make me offended if changes in the details are proposed. I hope there will be some discussion, and I hope it will be favourable, of the general principle of finding a way to provide for the Canadian House of Commons a continuing Speakership and I hope we can find a way to keep in the chair the illustrious occupant we have at the present time.
May I conclude my remarks by simply pointing out that there are four things in particular that I believe are problems related to this whole question, all four of them being problems that my bill solves. In the first place, to become a continuing Speaker one cannot be just a choice that was

October 29, 1971
Designation of Speaker
picked out somewhere; he has to have been a Member of Parliament elected in the first place in the ordinary way. My bill so provides.
In the second place a Speaker, once elected to the chair, does not automatically become a continuing Speaker; he has to prove himself through at least two sessions. This is called for in my bill.
In the third place, although my bill makes provision for a continuing situation it does not deny the right of each succeeding Parliament to make its choice. The good Speaker of one Parliament is there for the next Parliament to choose, but that new Parliament does not have to take him unless it, too, is satisfied.
My final point is that my bill makes it possible for a constituency that has done so well by electing a person who can fill the chair also to be a constituency that would have the right, in two years or so, to choose a member who would speak for it on the floor. This is achieved by the vacancy that is declared and the by-election that is to be held, as set out in Bill C-52.
I present the bill and its various points believing it is a matter that is of interest not only to members but to all Canadians who are concerned with the good image and the good functioning of Parliament, and I hope the debate on the bill this afternoon will be in that vein.

First of all, may I revert to my reference to semantics and say that I do not like the word "permanent". I prefer "continuing". Perhaps the difference is not as meaningful to my hon. friend as it is to me.
The second point is that we have that situation now. Somebody excellent occupies the chair. A Parliament lasts for two, three or four years. Parliament is dissolved and the Speaker is out, so to speak, and we must go through the process of electing another Speaker. I think that giving ourselves the right to arrange for the Speaker to continue from Parliament to Parliament makes good sense, both for the Speaker and for ourselves. There must be what my parliamentary secretary to my right calls a probationary period in which we make sure that the

person we have chosen is as good as we thought he would be.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. My question relates to the second Parliament in which Mr. Speaker might serve. speechtext:
May I say right from the start that I am unequivocally opposed to the idea of this bill. Let me make that clear from the beginning. I realize what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is trying to achieve, yet somehow there is a fatal flaw in the whole idea. First, although I should like to read copiously from a certain book I hold I shall content myself with reading part of what is printed inside the dust-jacket. It ought to be on the record, and reads as follows:
The Speaker is the representative of an institution which is a mocrocosm of the British nation and his prestige is immense. As the historic guardian of its privileges and its spokesman in its relations with the Crown, the House of Lords and authorities and persons outside Parliament, he is approached with ceremony and deference. His is a high and lonely office, above sectional interests and immune from party influences, and an extremely onerous one. He presides over debates, maintains discipline, interprets Standing Orders and gives rulings, and in addition has many administrative duties.
The idea of an impartial Speaker is a modern one.
That is the point I want to emphasize.
From the end of the fourteenth century, when the Speaker's name first appeared in records, he was for more than 250 years the King's man and as such liable to sudden rises to power and even quicker, sometimes fatal, falls.
October 29, 1971

If I may interpose, seven of them lost their heads.
After the Civil War the office became the perquisite of the government of the day and things began to improve, though of one Speaker it could still be said that 'nothing can exceed the badness of his character even in this bad age'. Great Speakers stalk the pages: Onslow, who served for a record thirty-three years in the eighteenth century and who is largely responsible for the modem concept of the Speaker; and Peel who, with his austere personality and splendid figure, dominated the House like a great actor and whose very presence was sufficient to quell disorder. Less happily, there was Speaker Gully who, in one of the House's worst moments, called in the police in 1901 to remove some recalcitrant Irish members.
There have been included in the Hansard of Westminster, in the Hansard of this House, in the Australian Hansard and the New Zealand Hansard very fine passages about the duties and responsibilities of the Chair. I have a quote from one of the recent Speakers of the New Zealand House on this point. It is noteworthy, however, that most of those speeches were made by members who did not occupy the chair. One ought to know that such paragons of virtue are exceedingly rare. One of the best descriptions of the duties, responsibilities and qualities of the Speaker is to be found in the Hansard record of this House for the year 1935. It is recorded in an exchange that took place between the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Bennett, and the returning Prime Minister, Mr. King, during the only really contested election for the office of Speaker. The contest had arisen as the result of some action taken rather precipitously by the Speaker-designate.
I hope the House will forgive me if some of my views are subjective. May I say that Mr. Speaker derives his authority and the respect of the members of this House from essentially being one of them. To my mind he is the first among peers, and to be first among peers he must be one of the peers; he must be one of the members of the House. I have always believed that.
There have been motions and bills presented in the British House and elsewhere supporting the idea that has been advanced, with some variations, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In Britain they wanted to call the Speaker the hon. member for St. Stephen's Hall. However, as soon as a member is elected to a position in which he is not one of the members of the House he becomes a super-official and is not one of the members. To my mind that is a fatal flaw. Even though the Speaker may represent a pseudo constituency, that is only a thin camouflage. Saying that he is elected to represent the constituency of Parliament Hill only thinly camouflages what he is.
One quality that we want of a Speaker is that he shall be scrupulously impartial. To be scrupulously impartial he must be independent-independent of government and independent of the opposition. This independence is fairly apparent in many ways in the United Kingdom where the custom has grown up that changes in government do not bring changes in the Speaker's office unless the Speaker has conducted himself in a completely unacceptable manner; otherwise he is expected to continue in office.
I recall what happened when the Labour government came to power in 1945. There is a famous story about the then Speaker. He was at King's Cross railway station, on his way home, and met Mr. Ernest Bevin, a minister in the Labour government. Mr. Bevin asked the Speaker,
Designation of Speaker
"Where are you going?" The Speaker replied, "I am going home to my constituency." "And what are you going to do there?" Mr. Bevin asked. The Speaker said, "Well, I am no longer wanted; isn't that so?" Mr. Bevin, who was a senior member of the then new Labour government, said, "Of course not. Don't be silly. Go back to your office; that is where you belong." I have paraphrased the story.
A little over a year ago I had the pleasure of seeing the only Labour Speaker of the House of Commons elected under a Conservative government. At that time there was no question that there would be any change. There has now been a change. The Speaker was nominated from government ranks only because Dr. King, the former Speaker, resigned for reasons of health. There is only one minor flaw in the British House. For the past year or two it has been said that at the end of a Speaker's term if is automatic that he shall be given a peerage. However, there is also the determination of his pension. What shall be the quantum of his pension? There has been a natural inclination to be rather pleasant to all members so that Mr. Speaker's pension will go through without any difficulty. I suggest it is a human failing, but that has been a trait.
Let us follow the procedures suggested by Bill C-252. An hon. member elected as Speaker of this House has, shall we say, a probationary period of two years. He must then wait and see whether the shoe fits. Will there be a resolution on the order paper proposing him as the hon. member for Parliament Hill? What will assure him of that? The bill is silent. Whose resolution will it be? Will it be that Mr. Speaker is appointed by government resolution? Mr. Speaker is the presiding officer of this House.

speechtext: So it cannot be a government resolution.

subtopic: DESIGNATION OF SPEAKER AS MEMBER FOR PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
How does a resolution get on the order paper to guarantee debate and that it will be taken up? Does it have precedence at the time of an election? Parliament will have met but the new session will not have started. There are some procedural difficulties. Will the resolution come after informal discussions through normal channels between the opposition and the government? This is a point. Human nature being what it is, there is a very grave danger that we will see in that section some equivocal acts in the mind of the occupant of the chair to guarantee that resolution appearing on the order paper next year.
During the first two years, is Mr. Speaker going to be independent of government? He may incur the wrath of the government or even the wrath of the opposition. He may incur the wrath of the government by a tough decision which is right. In recent years we have seen some reactions from government as the result of decisions by the Chair. Displeasure has been expressed in no uncertain terms. As a result, the House will suffer. I am concerned about the effect on the House and the protection of members on both sides, the protection of members one against the other, the private member from the government and the government from the opposition.
It is quite a job to protect the rights of this House. Mr. Speaker must not merely act as a referee and let the

October 29, 1971
Designation of Speaker
players slug one another as long as they do so above the belt. That is not the position of Mr. Speaker: he is much more than that. He must protect one member from another on both sides of the House. I wish to read what was said by Mr. Speaker Algie of the New Zealand House:
Since I have been in this House, I have listened with pleasure to a very great number of extremely able debaters and I have noted that the best of them are brief, terse, concise, relevant, and constructive. I have noted also that in their best moments they have been supremely polite, courteous, and free from personalities. That is the standard, honourable members, that we would like to attain and which the public would like us to reach.
I subscribe to that view. In order to achieve it, Mr. Speaker must take that attitude toward hon. members. By qualifying through a probationary period, Mr. Speaker's position might be very difficult. I come to a very practical problem, namely, the decision of an hon. member to accept an invitation to become Mr. Speaker. It has always been difficult. I assure hon. members that I wrestled with the problem. For a younger man it means a political derailment. Once Mr. Speaker takes the first step to the chair he must put aside partisan politics. There is no caucus, no special friends in any caucus and no political meetings. He becomes like Caesar's wife; there cannot be a finger of reproach pointed at him in this regard. This affects a person. Having occupied the chair I can assure hon. members that it still affects me in many ways.
Where does a man relatively young in service go from the chair unless there is to be a continuation? Is it going to be from the chair to the other place? That has been the record of a number of Speakers in this House, men of senior years. Is it going to be as some, myself included, who because of circumstances went from the chair into the cabinet? There is nothing wrong with that. I have seen the reverse, from the cabinet into the chair. The Speaker of the British House is a former cabinet minister. Former Speakers of this House have been chief whips of the government party.
What is to be the Speaker's career after the chair? One of the most serious deficiencies is that nothing is provided at the end of the road for Mr. Speaker. The pension scheme was thin; it is even thinner now. I think what we do is scandalous. Mr. Speaker as to abandon his private career. Being Speaker is a 150 per cent job. If Mr. Speaker is a young man he must consider his family, the future of his wife and himself. These are all factors to be considered.
But under this bill an hon. member who accepted the invitation to go into the chair would pass the probationary period, be elected by resolution, named to be the member for Parliament Hill and his constituency would disappear as far as he was concerned because his constituency would be represented by another member. We then have a general election. He is the representative for Parliament Hill. He does not go through a general election. There is a change of government, and where is he? There is no guarantee that he is going to continue, and he is out of the House.

speechtext: His guarantee is the decency of Parliament.

speechtext:
He is out of the House when he has taken the step that all hon. members have taken. They have made a conscious decision in many instances to give up business or professional careers. They have dedicated themselves to becoming Members of Parliament on behalf of their constituents, to a career in Parliament, that is, a career in public life. Again, the Speaker does not know. How is he to know he is going to carry on? There is a new administration. Remember, if this bill becomes law there is no alternative open to him, no certainty that a new administration would come along and accept Mr. Speaker. I much prefer the British system which we have seen put into practice following the last election, the steps which were taken at that time, albeit tentative.
It seems to me that now Parliament is a year-round proposition and has been for some years, and we have taken this tentative step, if Mr. Speaker indicates he wishes to continue as a member of a constituency he is not officially opposed and he does not contest the election. And let me tell you that the status of Mr. Speaker in his constituency during election time is very high. Other people can campaign on his behalf. It seems to me this does not put him at a disadvantage as far as the election is concerned.
So on a number of grounds I cannot endorse the proposal before us. First, I find that the last part of the probationary period would be very difficult for Mr. Speaker and I think deleterious to the interests of this House. I wish to be perfectly objective here without considering the personality of any man who has been in the chair.
Second, when we see a change in administration or even if there were a continuance of the same administration, what guarantee is there that the man who is in the position of the member for Parliament Hill, the outgoing Speaker, will be asked by the new administration to resume the chair? Suppose he has been called upon to make some very hard decisions-and sometimes they are very hard, decisions which incurred the wrath of the leader of the government party? That has happened and it will happen again in the future. It seems to me that by developing a system where by if Mr. Speaker has been conducting his office to the best of his ability and if, by reason of health and so forth, he is willing to continue, and if we also make sure in due course, as a major reform to come, that there is a proper pension available for him, we shall achieve what we want to achieve by way of an independent, continuing Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members have had the benefits of listening to a good discussion by two of the most experienced members of this House. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has not sought to retreat from the difficulties of the proposal he is advancing. His solutions to some of those difficulties are ingenious. On the other hand, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has not only portrayed for us the intrinsic difficulties of this proposal but has made specific comments critical of the solutions proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I begin my remarks by suggesting that we are discussing something which is highly important to the work of

this chamber and to parliamentary government in this country. It seems to me that this is the kind of proposal which should be referred to a committee in order that it may be studied further. I am surprised that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has suggested it should go to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs rather than to the distinguished committee of which we both are members. But I attribute this to his well known modesty.

subtopic: DESIGNATION OF SPEAKER AS MEMBER FOR PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
In this debate today, above all others, one should not say anything which could be considered as the least critical of the decision of the Chair and the officers of the House.
All hon. members are aware that we have made many important and constructive changes affecting the office of the Speakership even in the brief time during which I and others who first came here in 1968 have been in the House. To begin with, an important tradition has been supplanted. Formerly it was a tradition of Parliament that, after an election, a new Speaker should be chosen. I understand that it was also a tradition that the Speakership should alternate between a person whose mother tongue was English and a person whose mother tongue was French. But if I am not mistaken, it was determined for the first time before the election of 1968 that it would be advantageous to ask Mr. Speaker to continue in office. Arrangements were made between the parties during the election of 1968 which permitted Mr. Speaker to continue in office unembarrassed by a major political contest.
Other changes have been made which have increased the independence and the role of Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the most significant was the change in the rules which prohibited appeals from the Speaker's rulings. We know that the terms of Standing Order 26-a great favourite of hon. members opposite-having to do with emergency debate have also been revised so as to place much greater discretion in the hands of Mr. Speaker when determining which debates shall be allowed and the manner in which those decisions should be reached. One could mention other important changes which have been made in the rules conferring greater discretion on Mr. Speaker-for example, those dealing with the question period.
As we approach this debate we must realize that the force of recent opinion in this Parliament and, I suggest, also in the country has been in favour of creating a situation where the independence of the Speakership can be assured. This is the occasion that gave rise to the present debate and I think we are all equally concerned to find the best method of achieving this independence in the future.
I believe that the rules of this House, if not the rules of good manners, prevent me from saying anything more than the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre and Edmonton West have said about the present Speaker, but perhaps I might just say this. His distinction in his office
Designation of Speaker
is an added reason why all members of the House are now seeking and striving to find a way of ensuring the continuity of an independent Speakership of excellence and great quality. We must realize that, more than any other member of the House, the Speaker faces certain problems of membership. He is detached from many of the concerns of ordinary life. Under present circumstances, where Parliament sits for many months of the year, the Speakership itself is more than a year-round office.
In addition to this, in his office as Speaker he is deprived of any of the usual political arrangements that maintain contact in his constituency. At each election he faces the problem of determining how to go to the people and seek reaffirmation of his mandate when, by the very nature of his office, he is prevented during his term from participating in any of the usual activities associated with membership of this House.
If I might be permitted a personal observation, it has been my privilege as a member of this House to represent a constituency which lies beside that of Mr. Speaker. In addition, my provincial colleague during most of my term has been Speaker of the Ontario House. I am well aware of the feeling-which is not entirely justified, I must say- on the part of the people in the constituencies that a person who is Speaker is not representative of his constituents in the same sense as an ordinary member. I say that this feeling is not entirely justified because I have been able to observe rather closely how well the respective Speakers of this House and of the Ontario House have represented their constituents. But none the less the feeling persists and it is one which in a democratic society has to be recognized.
Coming more directly to the motion before us, we are all well aware of the history and traditions of the British Speakership. At least, we are well aware of them in general, though I think there is a certain mythology which attaches to the Speakership at Westminster. There are a great number of people in this country who believe there is a permanent Speakership at Westminster. People believe that there is a seat that is set aside for the Speaker. We know that this is not so. In fact, the independence of the Speakership at Westminster is the product of a long history, some of which might be regarded as fortuitous.
It happens that no Speaker since, I think, the year 1710 has been defeated in an election at Westminster. It also happens that for more than 180 years there has never been a contest in the House of Commons at Westminster over the election of a Speaker. As I understand it, this has been removed from all types of partisan consideration. In each election in the United Kingdom the Speaker stands as a candidate in his constituency and a determination has to be made by all political parties whether or not there will be a contest or whether there will be an acclamation. In the early years of this century, perhaps for almost 50 years, Speakers were acclaimed, but I believe the practice which has prevailed since 1945 is that British Speakers have gone through contested elections.
It is said, and I think not without reason, that the situation that prevails in the United Kingdom is rather different from that which prevails in this country. There the territory is smaller, the opportunity of people who may be represented by the Speaker to have access to other Members of Parliament is much more apparent than it might

October 29, 1971
Designation of Speaker
be here. This is the reason for the added weight given to the arguments in this country for the creation of what might be called a fictitious constituency which Mr. Speaker might represent.
This matter, as hon. members I am sure know, has been studied in a number of different areas. The British Parliament in 1939 had a very select committee consider this problem, the members of which included Winston Churchill, David Lloyd George and other parliamentarians of great reputation. They concluded in their report that it was an artificial solution to create a fictitious constituency for the Speaker. This conclusion appears to have been reinforced by a short debate that occurred in the United Kingdom Parliament on April 24, 1963.
In our own Parliament, as all hon. members are aware, extensive consideration was given to procedural matters prior to the election of 1968 and a great deal of work was done by our predecessors and by various people who contributed to their deliberations. Professor Denis Smith of Trent University filed a report entitled, "The Speakership of the Canadian House of Commons: Some Proposals", published as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings for June 2, 1965. There we find in a full blown way- unhappily, I cannot refer to the report except briefly-the argument for the creation of a permanent Speakership in which the Speaker would represent an artificial constituency, perhaps called the constituency of Parliament Hill.
Another important academic contribution was made by Professor J. H. Aitchison, who gave extensive attention to the office of Speaker and whose findings were published and reported, among other places, in the Ottawa Citizen for April 19, 1963. His conclusions are roughly the same as those of Professor Smith and both of their studies are entitled, I think, to great weight in any consideration that we give to this question.
On the other hand, I might mention the views of two distinguished parliamentarians of our generation which are to the opposite effect. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), speaking in this House on May 20, 1965, as reported at page 1517 of Hansard, declared himself firmly against this idea. He said:
I do not believe in the principle that a constituency should be set up for the purpose of providing a Speaker. He would then cease to be the first Commoner that he is, because he would be there by choice and not election.
To the same effect are the words spoken by the then Prime Minister, Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, on May 19, 1965, as reported at page 1483 of Hansard as follows:
This possibility has its attractions, but it seems to me that it also has its disadvantages, and I am not sure that it would achieve the objective it was desired to achieve in putting it into effect. This device would certainly transform the Speaker from being an equal with his fellow members over whose deliberations he presides into-I say this in no derogatory sense-some type of parliamentary functionary, and I suggest that the change might even reduce the prestige of*your office.
Finally, I should like to refer to the important words spoken by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) at the time of the election of Mr. Speaker on September 12, 1968, as reported at page 3 of Hansard of that day. The Leader of the Opposition said:
The appointment of a permanent Speaker remains one of the necessary objectives of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary improvement. I hope we can all agree upon the urgency of taking action in this regard ... is urgent in that respect as well as for the regulation of parliamentary procedure that early consideration be given to alternative methods of removing the election of the Speaker from partisan considerations.
We face a difficult problem. The best method of providing continuity of the independent Speakership of this House is one which we should earnestly seek and search for. We should also seek a method which would guarantee to the person who holds the onerous responsibility of our Speaker the greatest measure of security and independence. For this reason I urge all hon. members to support this motion so that it may be more fully considered in committee.
